title: Statement on AI
text:
In the age where AI is increasingly involved not only in an academic setting, but also in our daily lives, it is both important and necessary to create and follow a personal policy regarding one’s AI use.
There are generally four outcomes when we are faced with a problem in which we might consider using AI to solve (Cipolli 2026). We can decide against using AI at all, verify its suggestions with our own background knowledge, blindly follow it towards a correct answer, or blindly follow it towards an incorrect answer. I believe that relying on AI for answers where we don’t completely understand its sources, methods, or concepts will lead to a society in which humans will lose their autonomy in the workforce, and eventually in their own lives. If we don’t do our own thinking, then our functions in the workplace and in academics will become obsolete.
However, using AI to help us overcome barriers, unexpected issues, or to explain certain concepts that help us along the way of solving a problem can be super beneficial. Rather than spending hours trying to fix a bug that human error may miss, AI can quickly scan an entire file and notice one wrong button that was pressed. Using AI to make our lives more efficient to pave the way for learning, rather than doing the learning for us, is a great way to become an ethical statistical practitioner, as mentioned in the Ethical Guidelines for Statistical Practice (American Statistical Association 2022).
Not only does unethical AI use harm us, it also indirectly harms the people who might rely on our work. Passing work done by AI as your own is both an issue of plaigiarism and responsibility, and others might trust and cite your work as authentic and true, when in reality they are now citing AI (American Statistical Association 2022). It is important that we stay honest with the people we collaborate with and disclose all AI use, with plans to remedy any instances of unethical AI use.




References

American Statistical Association. 2022. Ethical Guidelines for Statistical Practice. Committee on Professional Ethics.


Cipolli, William. 2026. AI Statement.

title: HW1
text:
A benefit of using the Wilcox signed rank test is that the researchers don’t have to assume normality for the underlying population distribution, as that is unknown and the sample size is not large enough for the CLT. However, there are a few concerns to using this test:

The data collected are proportions that represent the number of times the GWL dogs correctly retrieved the new toy when requested out of 12 requests. The fact that this data is discrete with only 13 possible unique observations leads to multiple tied observations in the data. Using the exact Wilcoxon distribution could be an issue due to having many ties, and the authors would need to account for them in order to use an accurate Wilcoxon distribution.
Due to n=10, the sample size is likely not large enough to use an asymptotic distribution because n would usually need to be at least 50. Because the authors didn’t specify which distribution they used, this could be an issue.
The boundedness of the range of the data (0, 1), and the fact that 4 dogs had a proportion of 1.000 is a concern for the symmetry assumption for the Wilcoxon signed rank test. We don’t know the underlying distribution, and we definitely don’t have evidence supporting that it might be symmetric from the sample data.

A one-sample t-test is constrained by the assumption that the population is normally distributed and the population variance exists, both of which we don’t know, and the sample size of n = 10 does not satisfy the CLT. Since the sample data is skewed left, we don’t have evidence that the population distribution is normally distributed from the sample data. Moreover, a one-sample z-test for proportions also does not have a sample size large enough for the CLT. Due to the issues with the sample size, I think the best choice would be to use an exact binomial test because we don’t have to worry about our population data being normally distributed or about the CLT (relies on the binomial distribution). We can frame the data to be Bernoulli by interpreting each dog as a success if it retrieved the new toy correctly more than 50% of the time.



We are aiming to evaluate whether GWL dogs can correctly retrieve a new toy when requested better than chance (50%), aftering overhearing two people reference the object while not addressing the dog. n = 10 dogs were requested 12 times to retrieve the new toy, and our data present the proportion of times the dog correctly retrieved it.
Our null hypothesis is that H0: p = 0.50 and Ha: p > 0.50 and conducting a one-sided exact binomial test using alpha = 0.05, where a success means that the dog retrieved the new toy correctly more than half the time. We decided to use the exact binomial test because we violate no assumptions; our data does not satisfy the normality/CLT condition for a one-sample t-test, does not satisfy the symmetric assumption for a Wilcox signed rank test, and does not satisfy the sample size / CLT condition for a one-sample z-test for proportions.


Code
dat.dogs <- c(1.0000, 1.0000, 0.7500, 1.0000, 0.4167, 0.8333, 0.7500, 0.8333, 0.8333, 1.0000) # data 

successes <- sum(dat.dogs > 0.50)    # counts dogs better than chance (p > 0.50)
n <- length(dat.dogs)                # sample size (number of dogs)

test.result <- binom.test(x = successes,            # number of successes (p > 0.50)
                          n = n,                    # sample size (trials)
                          p = 0.50,                 # p0 = 0.50
                          alternative = "greater")  # one-sided test
(test.stat <- test.result$statistic) # test statistic


number of successes 
                  9 


Code
(p_val <- test.result$p.value)       # p-value


[1] 0.01074219


Code
(CI    <- test.result$conf.int)      # 95% confidence interval


[1] 0.6058367 1.0000000
attr(,"conf.level")
[1] 0.95


Our p-value (p_val = 0.0107) is less than alpha = 0.05, and we have statistically discernible evidence to conclude that the true proportion of correct retrievals is greater than 0.50. We can say with 95% confidence that the true proportion of correct retrievals of the new toy out of 12 requests lies between [0.61, 1.00].

title: HW1
text:
2 Question 2

2.1 Part a
The major issue with the binomial test here is that the number of trials is very low, in addition to already having a low sample size of n = 10. This might decrease the accuracy of the binomial distribution at predicting the true proportion of correctly selecting the new toy when requested. The conditions of the exact binomial test require that there be a fixed number of trials (2), and that each trial ends in a success or a failure. Additionally, the trials must be independent from one another, which is not satisfied in the 2 new toy trials, but would be satisfied if measuring the overall success of each dog as a separate 10 trials. Lastly, the binomial test assumes that the probability of success is the same across each trial, which is assumed to be p = 0.50.


2.2 Part b


Code
dat.dogs2 <- rep(1, 10) # data

n2 <- length(dat.dogs2)  # sample size
successes2 <- sum(dat.dogs2 == 1) # number of successes

test.result2 <- binom.test(x = successes2,            # data
                           n = n2,                    # number of trials
                           p = 0.25,                 # p0 = 0.50 for each dogs indiv. trial ^ 2 trials = 0.25
                           alternative = "greater")  # one-sided
test.result2$p.value


[1] 9.536743e-07


The probability of all 10 dogs successfully retrieving the new toy in both trials is around 0.00000095.


2.3 Part c


Code
n <- 10   # number of trials
p <- 0.25 # prob of success

mu_Y    = n*p             # mean of gaussian approx.
sigma_Y = sqrt(n*p*(1-p)) # standard dev of gaussian approx.

# P(B=b) = P(b - 0.50 < Y < b + 0.50) = P(Y<= b + 0.50) - P(Y<= b - 0.50)
# P(B=10) = P(10 - 0.50 < Y < 10 + 0.50) = P(Y<= 10 + 0.50) - P(Y<= 10 - 0.50)
(prob <- pnorm(10.5, mu_Y, sigma_Y) - pnorm(9.5, mu_Y, sigma_Y))


[1] 1.567447e-07


Yes, the probability obtained from the gaussian distribution approximation is around the same as the probability obtained from the binomial distribution. 0.00000095  0.00000016.


2.4 Part d
I think that, because all of the trials were a success, performing an inference might not be the best option due to having zero variability in the sample. Doing this inference, with no variability, will reject the null hypothesis unless p0 lies above some threshold. This meeans that the inference has less to do with the data and more to do with the chosen null hypothesis.
